title: Gym Sets With Rest
story: Your workout card lists sets, each tagged with a muscle group: L for legs, C for chest, B for back, and so on. Each time slot holds one set or a rest, and you may do the sets in any order. The coach's rule is that after a set for a group, at least rest other slots (other sets or rests) must pass before that group again. Finish in as few slots as possible.
task: Write fewestSlots(sets, rest). sets is a string of uppercase letters, one per set; equal letters are the same muscle group. Between two sets of the same group there must be at least rest other slots. Return the smallest total number of slots, counting rest slots, needed to do every set.
An empty card takes 0 slots. With rest = 0 there is no restriction.
constraints: sets contains only the letters A to Z

examples.explanation: One best order is L C _ L _ _ L, where _ is a rest. The three L sets force this length on their own, because the first and last L must be at least 2 × 3 = 6 slots apart, which makes 7 slots in total. C fills a gap but cannot shorten the schedule.
The order L C L C A B needs no rest, because every L and C is followed by a different group. There are 6 sets, so 6 is the minimum.

hints: In the first example, ignore C and place only the three L sets. How many slots do they force, whatever else is on the card?
The group with the most sets builds a frame: with m sets, needs m - 1 gaps of rest slots. Other sets go into the gaps. What if another group has just as many sets?

Each group tied for the most sets adds one slot at the end of the frame, so the frame is (m - 1) × (rest + 1) + k, where k is the number of tied groups. When could the answer be larger than the frame?

Count sets per group; let m be the largest count and k how many groups have it. If the other sets overflow the gaps, you never rest and the answer is the number of sets. Return max(sets.length, (m - 1) × (rest + 1) + k).
bruteForce: Trying every allowed order slot by slot grows exponentially, so even 30 sets is out of reach. Greedily picking the allowed group with the most sets left is correct, but it builds the whole schedule even though the answer depends only on how many sets the busiest groups have.

js: * @param {string} sets  one muscle-group letter per set
* @param {number} rest  slots required between two sets of the same group
py: def fewest_slots(sets: str, rest: int) -> int:

tests.note: two groups tie for most sets: forgetting the tie gives 7
more sets than the frame: the frame alone gives 7
taking groups in alphabetical order gives 6

js: // The busiest group(s) build a frame; other sets fill its gaps.
py: tied = sum(1 for c in counts if c == most)
# The busiest group(s) build a frame; other sets fill its gaps.
walkthrough: The group with the most sets is the bottleneck. Laid out as early as the rule allows, its sets form a frame: m - 1 blocks of rest + 1 slots, then the last set. Groups tied for most also need a slot after the last block. Every other set fits into the gaps, because it has fewer than m sets and can be spread across different blocks.
Trace "AAABBBCCD" with rest 1. The counts are A 3, B 3, C 2 and D 1, so m = 3 and k = 2, because A and B tie.
• The frame has (3 - 1) × (1 + 1) + 2 = 6 slots: A B | A B | A B.

• C, C and D still need places and the frame is full, so the blocks are widened: A B C | A B C | A B D. Widening only adds slots between equal groups, so it never breaks the rule. The leftovers are dealt out one group at a time, one set per block, cycling through the blocks, so two sets of one group always land a whole block apart.
• No rests are needed, so the answer is the number of sets, 9: max(9, 6).

There are two cases. If the other sets do not fill the gaps, rests are unavoidable and the frame is the answer. If they overflow the gaps, you never rest and the answer is the number of sets. The max covers both.
solution.timeWhy: One pass counts the sets, and after that there are at most 26 groups to look at.
solution.spaceWhy: The counts table has at most 26 entries.
solution.takeaway: When a cooldown or spacing rule applies to repeated items, find the most frequent item: its copies set a lower bound on the length, and everything else fills the gaps around them. Comparing that bound with the plain item count often gives the answer without building a schedule.
